analogy.source: Analogical transfer (Gick & Holyoak 1983): a structurally similar problem the learner already understands is what makes the present one tractable, where restating the present problem does not.
analogy.preference:
This student needs the problem connected to a different one they already
understand. Working inside the problem as posed leaves them unable to see its
shape.

PASS if the message presents a different problem or situation sharing the structure
of this one, and indicates what corresponds to what.

FAIL if the message stays entirely inside the problem as posed. FAIL if it offers a
comparison without saying which parts correspond. FAIL if the other situation is
decorative and carries none of the structure.

contrasting_cases.source: Contrasting cases (Schwartz & Bransford 1998; Marton's variation theory): the relevant distinction becomes visible when two cases differing in one respect are set side by side, and stays invisible when either is presented alone.
contrasting_cases.preference:
This student needs two cases side by side. A single case, however well chosen,
leaves them unable to tell which feature matters.

PASS if the message presents two cases together and points at the difference
between them that carries the lesson.

FAIL if the message presents a single case only. FAIL if it presents two without
naming what differs. FAIL if the difference it names is incidental rather than the
one the step turns on.

deep.source: Marton & Saljo (1976): deep approach -- intent to grasp the underlying meaning, seeking the reason behind a procedure rather than the procedure alone. Developed by Entwistle and Biggs.
deep.preference:
This student is after the reason, not just the move. A step with no reason behind
it teaches them nothing, because they cannot tell when it would apply again.

Find the clause in this message that says why something is true, or why it is the
right thing to do: a clause turning on because, since, so that, the reason is, this
works because, or similar.

PASS only if such a clause is present and what it justifies is a mathematical claim
or move in this problem.

FAIL if no such clause is present. Stating a rule, naming a property, or giving an
example is not a justification. A clause about why the teacher is asking a question
is not a justification. Asking the student to explain is not a justification.

error_focused.source: Learning from errors (Metcalfe 2017; VanLehn's repair theory), and the Error Flagging strategy in the TACT tutor-strategy taxonomy: the mistake has to be located before a correction can land, or the learner repeats it.
error_focused.preference:
This student needs their own mistake named before anything else. A correction
that does not first say what went wrong leaves them repeating it.

PASS if the message identifies the specific step, line or value in the student's
work that is wrong, before offering any further instruction.

FAIL if the message offers new instruction without locating an error in what the
student did. FAIL if it reports that something is wrong without saying which part.
FAIL if it treats the student's work as sound and simply carries on from it.

example_first.source: Worked-example effect and expertise reversal (Sweller; Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler & Sweller): a worked instance before the general rule helps the less expert learner, where the same sequencing is redundant or harmful for the more expert one.
example_first.preference:
This student needs something concrete before anything general. A rule stated in
the abstract does not land for them.

PASS if the message presents a concrete instance before any general rule appears: a
particular case carrying specific values, or a smaller version of the problem
walked through.

FAIL if the message opens with a rule, formula, identity or definition, or if it
offers no instance at all. Restating the problem, naming its structure, introducing
a symbol, defining a variable, or announcing that an example follows are all
descriptions rather than instances, and none of them satisfy this student.

executive.source: Nelson-Le Gall (1981, 1985): executive (expedient) help-seeking -- seeking to have the problem solved rather than to learn to solve it. Tied to dependency orientation.
executive.preference:
This student wants the next step handed to them. They are here to get the problem
moving, and a message that hands the decision back to them stalls them.

PASS if the message states the next step plainly enough for the student to act on
it.

FAIL if the next step is left for the student to work out, decide or supply. A
closing request for confirmation does not by itself cause a FAIL when the step
itself was stated.

instrumental.source: Nelson-Le Gall (1981, 1985): instrumental help-seeking -- seeking the minimum assistance needed to succeed independently, e.g. a hint or the principle behind a step, rather than the solution itself. Tied to mastery orientation.
instrumental.preference:
This student asks for help in order to do the work themselves. They want the
smallest push that lets them find the next step, and they disengage when the step is
handed to them.

Identify what the message tells the student to work with: the operation to perform,
the quantity to use, or the sub-goal to reach.

PASS only if the message names none of those, so that deciding what to work with is
still the student's to do.

FAIL if the message names the operation, the quantity, or the sub-goal, even when it
is phrased as a question, and even when the student must still carry out the
arithmetic.

rule_first.source: Expertise reversal effect (Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler & Sweller 2003), the other pole of the worked-example interaction: for the more expert learner an instance without the stated principle is redundant, and the general rule is what makes the instance reusable.
rule_first.preference:
This student wants the governing rule stated first, and finds a worked instance
hard to reuse when the principle behind it is left unsaid.

PASS if the message opens by stating the general rule, identity, definition or
property it relies on, before any specific numbers.

FAIL if it opens with specific numbers or an informal analogy, or if it never
states the general rule it is using.

surface.source: Marton & Saljo (1976): surface approach -- intent to reproduce the procedure with the minimum engagement necessary, treating the task as something to get through.
surface.preference:
This student wants only what is needed to proceed, one piece at a time, and stops
reading long messages.

Count the things this message asks the student to do or think about.

PASS only if that count is exactly one, and the message ends after it.

FAIL if the count is two or more. FAIL if the message continues past the single
request with praise, a summary, an invitation, or anything else.
